title: Backward-compatible deployments
description: Design API and contract changes so old and new versions can coexist safely during rolling updates.

data.text: In a rolling update, old and new instances of an application run at the same time. If the new version changes an API contract, old instances may crash or produce incorrect results. Backward-compatible deployments ensure that every contract change can be understood and handled by both the current and previous versions of the system.
This lesson covers API versioning strategies, tolerant reader patterns, event schema evolution, and how to apply these techniques in CI/CD pipelines without manual coordination.

The tolerant reader pattern says that consumers should ignore fields they do not understand and producers should never remove fields without a deprecation period. This simple rule lets systems evolve independently. A new service can start sending an extra field, and old consumers continue working. An old service can continue sending a deprecated field, and new consumers ignore it.

data.title: Tolerant JSON payload
data.content: Version 2 of the API adds an optional 'currency' field. Version 1 consumers ignore it; Version 2 consumers default missing currency to USD.

data.title: Common approaches
items: URI versioning: /api/v1/orders and /api/v2/orders. Clear but duplicates routes.
Header versioning: Accept header carries the version. Cleaner URLs but harder to test with curl.
Query parameter: ?version=2. Visible in logs but easy to implement.

data.title: Prefer additive changes
data.text: Adding fields is backward compatible. Renaming, removing, or changing the type of an existing field is not. If you must make a breaking change, introduce a new version and keep the old version running until all clients have migrated.

Event-driven systems have the same compatibility problem, but the consequences are worse. If one consumer crashes because of a bad event, the entire queue can stall. Use schema registries such as Azure Event Hubs schema registry or Confluent Schema Registry to enforce compatibility rules before events reach consumers.

terms.definition: New consumers can read old producer data.
Old consumers can read new producer data.
A central service that stores, validates, and versioned message schemas.

items.text: API changes are additive or versioned; no breaking changes without a new API version.
items.hint: Review pull requests for removed or renamed fields.

items.text: Consumers ignore unknown fields and supply defaults for missing fields.
Event schemas are validated against compatibility rules before publishing.
items.hint: Use BACKWARD or FULL compatibility in your schema registry.

items.text: Old API versions remain available until all clients are confirmed migrated.
items.hint: Track usage by client version in your analytics.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Rolling updates require contracts that both old and new versions can handle.
Additive changes are inherently backward compatible.
Breaking changes need a new version and a client migration plan.
Schema registries enforce compatibility for event-driven systems.
data.takeaway: Backward compatibility is not accidental; it is a design choice enforced through code review and tooling.

items.question: What if I cannot avoid a breaking change?
items.answer: Introduce a new versioned endpoint or event type, keep the old one running, and redirect new clients. Deprecate the old version with a clear timeline and communicate it to all consumers.

items.question: How long should I keep old API versions?
items.answer: Keep them until analytics show zero traffic from old clients. For internal APIs, a few sprints is usually enough. For public APIs, provide at least one year of notice before retiring a major version.
